title: Orthopedics: Compartment Syndrome, Fat Embolism, Hip Precautions

questions.stem: A client with a new leg cast has pain not relieved by morphine that gets worse when the toes are gently stretched. What is most likely happening?
questions.explanation: B is correct: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are early signs of compartment syndrome. A misses the danger. C causes confusion, low oxygen, and a rash. D is a hip replacement problem.

questions.stem: Which are early signs of compartment syndrome? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pain out of proportion to the injury
Pain when the muscle is passively stretched

questions.explanation: A, B, C, and D are correct: these are the early signs. E and F are late signs; by the time the pulse is gone, the muscle may be dying.

questions.stem: A client shows early signs of compartment syndrome. How should the limb be positioned?
questions.explanation: B is correct: keep the limb at heart level, not raised. A and D both cut blood flow to a starving compartment. C is not taught.

questions.stem: Which actions fit compartment syndrome care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Loosen the dressing or cast, per order
Recheck circulation, movement, and feeling often
Wait until the pulse is lost before calling

questions.explanation: A, B, C, and D are correct: notify, remove ice, loosen per order, recheck often, and prepare for surgery. E waits for a late sign.

questions.stem: When does fat embolism usually appear after a long-bone or pelvic fracture?
questions.explanation: B is correct: fat embolism shows up one to three days after a long-bone or pelvic fracture. A, C, and D are not the timing taught.

questions.stem: Which finding helps separate fat embolism from a blood clot in the lungs?

options.text: Tiny red spots on the chest and neck

questions.explanation: C is correct: the rash of tiny red spots on the chest and neck separates fat embolism from a blood clot in the lungs. A, B, and D can occur with both.

questions.stem: Two days after a femur fracture, a client has new confusion, an oxygen saturation of 88%, and red spots on the chest. What is the first action?

options.text: Give oxygen, then call rapid response
Reorient and recheck in one hour

questions.explanation: A is correct: this is likely fat embolism, so oxygen first, sit them up, and get help fast. B delays care. C: sit them upright. D can hide worsening confusion and breathing.

questions.stem: After a posterior-approach hip replacement, which are classic precautions? Select all that apply.

options.text: Don't bend the hip past 90 degrees
Sit in a low, soft chair

questions.explanation: A, B, and C are correct: no bending past 90 degrees, no crossing the legs, and no turning the toes inward, always per the surgeon's orders. D and E are wrong: use a raised toilet seat and a high chair.

questions.stem: After a hip replacement, which finding suggests the new hip has popped out?
questions.explanation: A is correct: watch for a shortened, rotated leg. B, C, and D are not the dislocation sign taught.

questions.stem: Which equipment helps keep a new hip in place after a posterior-approach replacement?

options.text: Ice on the hip at all times
A pillow under the knees to bend the hip

questions.explanation: A is correct: use an abduction pillow, a raised toilet seat, and a high chair. B and D bend the hip too far. C is not a hip precaution.
